source: Kambhampati (2000) Planning Graph as a (Dynamic) CSP: Exploiting EBL, DDB and other CSP Search Techniques in Graphplan (JAIR 12)
finding: Adds explanation-based learning (EBL, short no-goods from failure explanations) and dependency-directed backtracking (DDB) to Graphplan. Speedups depend strongly on domain. This fixes an effect size for no-goods outside SAT (gap 8).
numbers: Speedup of EBL/DDB over plain Graphplan: 1.6x in blocks world up to 120x in logistics (Att-log-a unsolved by plain Graphplan after 40+ hours cpu). Abstract claims up to 1000x on some problems. Rocket-ext-a backtracks 5181K plain vs 2004K with EBL/DDB. Problem set: blocks, rocket, logistics, gripper, tower, ferry, TSP, Hanoi.
quote: EBL/DDB techniques can offer quite dramatic speedups from 1.6x in blocks world all the way to 120x in the logistics domain
limits: Lisp implementation, old hardware, 2000-era benchmarks. Table 1 text is partly garbled in the PDF extract, so only figures quoted in prose or cleanly readable are used.
agent_relevance: Outside SAT the gain from short no-goods is 1.6x to 120x, not one number. It is huge where failures have small causes and small where goals interact. Expect the same spread across our task families.

source: Kambhampati (2000) Planning Graph as a (Dynamic) CSP (JAIR 12), section 5.2 memo length
finding: The size of the speedup tracks how much the stored no-good shrinks after explanation. Where few goals take part in a failure, memos get much shorter and the speedup is large. In blocks world goals interact, memos shrink little, and the speedup is meager. This is a measurable boundary condition and a cheap test for gap 9.
numbers: Average memo length (EBL/DDB vs plain): Gripper-8 8.5 vs 23.9; Tower-5 7.5 vs 23.8; Ferry-6 6.9 vs 14.9; Att-log-a 10.15 vs 11.83; Rocket-ext-a 9.52 vs 11.3. Author says memo-length reduction is correlated perfectly with speedup. EBL+DDB vs DDB only: Att-log-a 120x, Tower-6 51x, Rocket-ext-a 21x, Gripper-8 1.94x, TSP-10 2.09x, Huge-Fct 1.19x.
quote: The reduction in average memo length is correlated perfectly with the speedups offered by EBL
limits: About 15 problems, one planner, correlation not a controlled test. Some table rows are misaligned in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Cheap G12 gate: run a few failures, let code compute the ratio of full state size to derived reason size. If the reason is not much shorter than the state, do not build a no-good store for this task family.

source: Kambhampati (2000) Planning Graph as a (Dynamic) CSP (JAIR 12), sections 5.5 and 6 on memoization cost
finding: Checking stored no-goods can itself dominate run time, and removing the store does not fix it. The paper argues Graphplan avoids the known storage-cost problem of EBL because it keeps only compact, selective no-goods (failed sets of activated goals).
numbers: Rocket-ext-a: plain Graphplan 19.4 min, of which 11.7 min (over half) is memo checking. Memo checking disabled: 16.5 min. EBL/DDB: 0.8 min. DDB with memo checking disabled: 2.4 min (3x slower than EBL).
quote: memo checking can sometimes be a significant fraction of the run-time of standard Graphplan
limits: Single instance for the breakdown. Hash lookup cost does not map to prompt tokens.
agent_relevance: Store size has a price. For an LLM the price is prompt tokens, so keep the store in code and show only entries that match the current state, as Graphplan checks memos only for the current goal set.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization (AAAI-98)
finding: Run lengths of complete backtrack search on hard instances follow heavy-tailed distributions. Random tie-breaking plus a cutoff and restart removes the tail and exploits a small chance of a very short run. They solved instances no deterministic run could. Formal result: the restart strategy has finite mean and variance even if the base procedure has infinite ones.
numbers: Logistics.d with Satz: deterministic run 108 minutes; best cutoff very low, success under 1% per run, about 1,800 backtracks in total per solution. Round-robin scheduling solved up to 18 teams vs 14 deterministic. Logistics-as-SAT extended from 1,141 to 2,160 variables, mean 95 s.
quote: Adding cutoffs and restarts to the search algorithm, however, both theoretically and empirically eliminate the heavy-tail and bound the mean.
limits: Counts are backtracks on CSP/SAT, not LLM calls. Table 1 columns are garbled in the PDF extract, so only prose figures are used.
agent_relevance: A restart only pays if run length is heavy-tailed. For an LLM agent this is an empirical question per task family, so log run lengths before adding a restart rule.

source: Gomes, Selman, Kautz (1998) Boosting Combinatorial Search Through Randomization (AAAI-98), counter-example instance
finding: Boundary condition. On one planning instance, no heavy tail appeared over a range of cutoffs and heuristic settings. Randomization helped only slightly. The authors say further work is needed to learn which problem traits give heavy tails.
numbers: Optimal equivalence setting 30%; mean cost 23 minutes after randomization.
quote: there was no evidence of a heavy-tailed distribution, and, therefore, randomization only slightly increases the effectiveness of Satz
limits: One instance. The deterministic baseline for this instance is not readable in the extract.
agent_relevance: Restarts are not a free win. Measure the spread of attempt lengths and successes before adding a restart rule to the schema.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: For LLMs, fresh independent attempts (the restart analogue with no memory) raise coverage smoothly, roughly log-linear in sample count over orders of magnitude, fitted by an exponentiated power law. This is indirect support for restart value; it does not test heavy-tailed run lengths. Selection without a real verifier does not keep up.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250 samples (single-attempt SOTA 43%). CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority voting or a reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%. GSM8K and MATH sets are 128 problems each.
quote: coverage increases from 82.9% with 100 samples to 98.44% with 10,000 samples
limits: Samples are independent with no lessons carried over, so this is pure restart, not CDCL restart with learned clauses. Small problem sets for math. Needs an automatic verifier to turn coverage into accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly answered. Cheap fresh restarts have strong value when a verifier exists. Open: whether carrying no-goods across restarts beats fresh samples at equal tokens.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: At equal compute (pass@t counts tokens including feedback), self-repair is often no better than sampling more first attempts, and sometimes worse at small budgets. Gains from more initial samples are consistent; gains from more repairs per sample are marginal. The bottleneck is the quality of the textual feedback, the analogue of conflict analysis.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Code Llama on APPS and HumanEval; budgets up to 50 samples. Repair success with GPT-4's own explanations 33.30% overall (Intro 42.64, Interview 19.33, Competition 3.67) vs 52.60% with human feedback (62.21, 45.67, 14.67); 40 failing programs, 16 participants, 2 feedback texts per program, 25 repairs per feedback. A stronger feedback model let Code Llama and GPT-3.5 beat both baseline and their own self-repair on APPS.
quote: the most important factor determining whether self-repair will lead to a correct program or not is the diversity of the base samples
limits: Code tasks with unit-test feedback. Repair is free text, not a formal no-good. Small human study.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2, indirect. Free-text reflection does not beat resampling at equal tokens, and its limit is diagnosis quality. A formal no-good store must be tested against plain resampling at equal tokens, not only against no memory.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings of ACL 2024)
finding: Backtracking to the true first-mistake step and resampling from there helps; backtracking to a random step helps much less and breaks more correct traces. This is the closest LLM test of backjumping to the responsible step (gap 6). LLMs are poor at finding that step themselves.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 5 tasks, 300 traces per task, 85% incorrect. Word sorting, oracle location: 11.11% of originally correct traces turned wrong, 23.53% of originally wrong traces turned right. Random location: 15.56% lost, 11.76% fixed. GPT-4 direct step-level mistake finding overall accuracy 52.87, the best of five models.
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Oracle location is human-labelled. Short CoT traces (5 to 24 steps). Compared against random location, not against retry from scratch at equal tokens. Only the word-sorting row is read cleanly from the extract.
agent_relevance: Backjumping to the right culprit roughly doubles the fix rate over a random cut, but only if the culprit can be found by code or a reliable check. LLM self-location is the weak link. Supports gap 10 rule: derive culprit and difficulty signals in code.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location, section 5.1 accuracy needed
finding: Gap 7 analogue. Simulated mistake finders of varying accuracy show how reliable a failure signal must be. Losses on correct traces plateau near 65% finder accuracy, and for most tasks gains exceed losses at about 60-70% accuracy. A small trained classifier did not reach the needed level.
numbers: Simulated classifier: true location X% of the time, random wrong location otherwise, X from 0 to 100. Out-of-domain classifier PaLM 2 Otter beat 3-shot PaLM 2 Unicorn on 4 of 5 held-out tasks but stayed below the threshold.
quote: the losses in accuracy begins to plateau at 65%
limits: Locating a mistake is not the same as deriving a lesson. Wrong locations are drawn from the dataset distribution. Five tasks.
agent_relevance: Rough threshold: a failure signal right less than about 60% of the time makes backjumping a net loss on correct traces. A no-good store with a bad signal prunes true answers. Use only high-precision checks.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works well where reliable external feedback exists. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Many positive results used oracle information or weak baselines.
numbers: Qualitative survey; no pooled effect size.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Covers work up to early 2024. The reliable external signal is the condition, which a no-good store also needs.
agent_relevance: Gap 7. A lesson store must be fed by a code-checked failure signal. Text-only judge feedback is not a safe source of no-goods.

source: Su et al. (2025) Mistake Notebook Learning: Batch-Clustered Failures for Training-Free Agent Adaptation (arXiv 2512.11485)
finding: Gap 4 evidence on a larger model. Always-on memory harms; a store with an accept-if-improves gate does not. On DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp two memory baselines lowered scores badly, while MNL kept the baseline by keeping zero entries when updates did not help. MNL commits an update only if net improvement B>0 on the batch.
numbers: AppWorld task success, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp: vanilla 73.2, Memento 64.2 (56 entries), ACE 44.6 (8 entries, 6,902 tokens), MNL 73.2 (0 entries). Mind2Web: vanilla 15.49 task success / 66.32 step accuracy, Memento 0.34 / 12.60, ACE 15.82 / 57.80, MNL 18.86 / 67.55 (12 entries, 395 tokens). Qwen3-8B Mind2Web: vanilla 1.35, Memento 0.00, ACE 0.00, MNL 2.02.
quote: The memory update is accepted if and only if B > 0
limits: Single group; no confidence intervals; small N on AppWorld. Memento and ACE were reimplemented by the authors.
agent_relevance: Confirms the Sentry harm finding on a bigger model and gives a fix: gate every store update on a measured gain, and let the store stay empty.

source: Su et al. (2025) Mistake Notebook Learning, ablations and think-enabled models
finding: Abstracting over a batch of failures beats per-failure lessons, and extra epochs overfit the store. With reasoning-enabled models the gain is small, so benefit shrinks as the base model gets stronger.
numbers: KaggleDBQA: batch size 1 to 16 raised accuracy 17% and cut memory size 3x (24% with 69 entries at batch 1 vs 28% with 23 entries at batch 16). Epoch 1 test 28.1%, epoch 2 test 23.2% while train rose to 62.1%. Think-enabled: Qwen3-8B Mind2Web task success 1.01 to 1.35; DeepSeek-Reasoner AppWorld 75.0 to 76.2; Qwen3-8B AppWorld 8.9 to 10.7. GSM8K Qwen3-8B 91.8 to 93.9 (SFT 94.3). AIME24/25 Pass@32 30/23 vanilla to 33/30 with 51 entries.
quote: Single-epoch training yields the highest test accuracy
limits: Small test sets (KaggleDBQA 185 test items). Gains on think models are about 1 point, probably inside noise.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4. Keep stores small and general, merge near-duplicates, and expect small gains on strong reasoning models. Weakens the case for a large store of per-failure no-goods.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Trajectory-Informed Memory Generation for Self-Improving Agent Systems (IBM, arXiv 2603.10600)
finding: Gaps 3 and 4 on a GPT-4.1 agent. Tips (including recovery tips from failures) retrieved by trigger help, but a restrictive top-k put the agent below the no-memory baseline. Gains concentrate on the hardest tasks and on consistency across task variants. Loose or wrong retrieval adds noise.
numbers: AppWorld test-normal, GPT-4.1. Baseline TGC 69.6, SGC 50.0. Subtask tips with LLM-guided selection TGC 73.2 (+3.6), SGC 64.3 (+14.3). Cosine threshold 0.6, no top-k: TGC 72.0 (+2.4), SGC 62.5 (+12.5). Threshold 0.5 with top-3: TGC 66.7 (-2.9), SGC 48.2; Difficulty 3 TGC 46.0 (-8.0 vs baseline). Difficulty 3 SGC 19.1 to 47.6 (+28.5 pp, 149% relative) with task-level tips.
limits: Technical report, one benchmark, small partitions, no confidence intervals. Tips are free text from an LLM, not formal no-goods. The report contains a placeholder reference.
agent_relevance: A frontier-class model gains when retrieval is matched by trigger and not cut to a small fixed k. The knob is match quality, not list length. Nothing here supports k=3 or k=5 as a default.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search Unifies Reasoning, Acting, and Planning in Language Models (LATS)
finding: Gaps 1 and 6 reference point. In search with stored reflections of failed branches, removing reflection costs little on HotPotQA, and on WebShop the reflections were often generic and the agent got stuck in local minima.
numbers: HotPotQA EM, ReAct base, n=5 children, k=50 trajectories: LATS 0.63, no reflection 0.58 (drop 0.05), DFS variant 0.42, no LM heuristic 0.37, RAP 0.54, ToT 0.39. Reflexion's gain over ReAct on the same task is 0.19. WebShop: k=30 trajectories with ReAct and with Reflexion gave similar scores.
quote: generated reflections are often generic and do not provide useful feedback
limits: GPT-3.5-era models. Reflection is free text, not a formal no-good.
agent_relevance: Free-text reflection is a weak no-good. Most of the lift in tree search comes from search and value function, so exploration control in code is the cheaper win and lessons are a smaller add-on.

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
finding: Gap 7 context. Single weak verifiers are noisy, poorly calibrated and have high false-positive rates; naive aggregation is not enough. Weighted ensembling of many verifiers lifts selection accuracy a lot, but the headline weights are computed with test labels (oracle); with only 1% labels accuracy drops.
numbers: Llama 3.3 70B generator with Weaver over 70B-or-smaller judges and reward models: 87.7% average across MATH500, GPQA Diamond, MMLU College and MMLU Pro, vs GPT-4o 69.0% and o3-mini 86.7%. Success rates of individual verifiers differ by up to 37.5%. With only 1% labelled data (0.01n) accuracy drops 20.1% on average (Table 17, as stated in text).
quote: these weak verifiers produce noisy, inconsistent scores, often exhibit poor calibration, and suffer from high false positive rates
limits: Selection among samples, not no-good learning. Benchmarks are multiple-choice or math with a known answer set.
agent_relevance: If a failure signal cannot be a hard code check, combine several independent weak checks before any lesson enters the store. One weak judge is not enough.
